az_coop_the_2.blurb: A compact, bowl-shaped alcove tucked just east of The Bowling Alley in the Farmhouse zone of southern Arizona, at roughly 5,500 feet. All eleven routes are bolted sport lines on walls of about 45 to 85 feet. The grades start around 5.10 and cluster in the low to mid 5.12 range, so this is a place for strong sport climbers rather than beginners. Because the cove curves around, a couple of its walls usually stay shaded through the summer, and the north-facing Farmhouse walls remain cool and dark in winter. The walk in is a steep, cairned hillside trail that is still being developed and can be hard to follow.

az_titanic_the.blurb: A short, north-facing cliff perched on a hill beside a bend in the wash, in the Euro Dog Valley part of Queen Creek Canyon near Superior. It is a mixed bag of eleven climbs: a handful of boulder problems in the V2 to V3 range, a few bolted sport lines, and two trad routes, with most of the roped climbs around 5.10 and one easier line near 5.7. The wall is small, so it suits a quick session more than a full day. Getting there takes only a couple of minutes on a cairn-marked path up from the wash.

az_reception_area_the.blurb: A zone of steep, featured sandstone where Oak Creek Canyon narrows into a slot, reached from the Cave Springs campground area south of Flagstaff. It sits just past the Outpatient zone and below the boulder scramble that leads up to the Doctor's Office. Most of the eleven routes are bolted sport lines, with a few trad routes mixed in, and the difficulty is demanding: nothing is easy, with grades starting at 5.10 and running up through the 5.11s and 5.12s into the low 5.13s. Expect sustained, technical face climbing on rock quality that varies from good to poor.

az_beale_st_east.blurb: The eastern half of Beale Street Wall on the northern edge of Kingman, a low-key bolted crag that is easy to reach from town. The wall is about 40 feet tall, nearly vertical and faces north, which keeps it in shade through the afternoon. All eleven routes are sport climbs with glued-in bolts, graded mostly from 5.7 through 5.10, so it works well for newer leaders, warm-ups and top-rope laps. Short routes and a quick walk make it a handy half-day stop rather than a destination crag.
az_beale_st_east.parking_note: Leave the car in the Camp Beale Springs lot, reached by turning off Fort Beale Drive onto Wagon Trail Road about a mile north of downtown Kingman.
az_beale_st_east.approach: From the lot, head west beneath the overhead power lines for about a quarter mile, stepping over an old wire fence to reach the wall. An alternative starts at the Camp Beale Loop trailhead further up Fort Beale Drive.

az_saddle_boulders.blurb: A small cluster of boulders in the Icecapades bouldering zone of the Phoenix area, sitting on a saddle between two low hills at about 1,600 feet. The centerpiece is a roughly 25-foot boulder with a long sloping rail about five feet up its main face. There are eleven problems, covering a wide spread from easy V0 up through the middle grades to a single V7, with several traverses among the better lines. The area is spread out and lightly visited, so expect some wandering on trails to find the right stone.
az_saddle_boulders.approach: Walk north toward the smaller hills, follow the valley between them, and continue up to the saddle where the boulders sit.
